previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis and severe asthma was admitted after developing hypercarbic respiratory failure during an asthma exacerbation, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. He was transferred to the ICU, where he was treated with sedation, paralysis, and antibiotics after bronchoscopy revealed influenza B, MSSA, and Serratia. He improved clinically, was successfully extubated, and transitioned to oral therapy. Imaging showed cirrhosis and a liver lesion requiring further evaluation with MRI. His home medications for cirrhosis and asthma were restarted. He was discharged to an extended care facility for rehabilitation with follow-up arranged for hepatology, pulmonology, and consideration of Xolair and sleep apnea evaluation.

Discharge Instructions:
Dear ___,

It was a pleasure taking care of you at the ___ 
___.

As you know, you were admitted to the inpatient Medicine service 
for shortness of breath, fevers, cough, and abdominal pain. In 
the Emergency Room, a chest x-ray showed that you had nothing 
urgently worrisome in your heart or lungs. Your peak flow values 
were reduced from your normal levels, and you required 
intravenous steroid, pain medication, and nebulized steroids to 
help relieve your shortness of breath. This was consistent with 
a diagnosis of asthma exacerbation. Your breathing continued to 
improve once you were in the hospital, and we gave you a 5-day 
course of oral steroid, nebulized steroids, and inhalers to help 
relieve your asthma exacerbation.

You also noted significant abdominal pain that was worst in the 
upper middle abdomen and radiated to your back. We started you 
on intravenous pain medications and intravenous fluids to manage 
your symptoms. A CT scan of your abdomen did not show any 
obvious source for your pain, and most of your lab tests were 
inconclusive. We then ordered an ultrasound scan of your liver 
and gallbladder, which was unremarkable as well. We then had you 
undergo a procedure which evaluates your esophagus, stomach, and 
small intestine by directly visualizing them. We found that you 
had a fungal infection of your esophagus and ulcers in your 
stomach that were due in part to a viral infection. You 
immediately began treatment for both with oral medications. You 
will continue to take these medications daily after discharge 
until indicated to help relieve your pain and clear the 
infections. We also sent various lab tests to further evaluate 
your infections. As we discussed, you are susceptible to the 
specific esophageal infection due to your use of inhaled 
steroids for asthma. Using a spacer and careful attention to 
hygiene may help prevent these types of infections in the 
future. Despite your improving breathing and throat/chest pain, 
you still maintained stable abdominal pain. To further assess 
this, you recently had a special type of MRI scan of your 
abdomen (MRCP), which evaluates your bile ducts and pancreas in 
great detail, for further assessment of your continued abdominal 
pain. On that imagine, we found a liver mass of unclear 
etiology. You will need to follow up with Dr. ___ as an 
outpatient to discuss a likely biopsy.

Proper methods of pain control are also very important for you. 
We discussed the importance of our goal of weaning you off 
narcotics. We successfully took a step-wise approach to this by 
initially stopping your intravenous narcotics, and then reducing 
the dose and frequency of your oral narcotics. It is important 
you follow-up closely with your primary care provider, Dr. ___, 
___ adhere strictly to his instructions regarding ___ in 
order to eventually get off narcotics permanently.

As we discussed with you during your hospital stay, we feel it 
is very important that you routinely see Dr. ___, as well as a 
liver specialist (hepatologist) and a lung specialist 
(pulmonologist) for careful monitoring of your liver disease and 
asthma. Close follow-up could help prevent future issues 
requiring hospitalization.

We wish you the best of luck. Take care.

Sincerely,
Your ___ Team

2.  Group of multiple nodules within segment 4A/B surrounding the gallbladder

by surrounding confluent hepatic fibrosis.

Short term MR imaging follow up of the liver is recommended in 3 months to
assess the dysplastic nodules and sub-cm focus of arterial hyperenhancement.
